chunks: The wudu is not broken except by what exits from the two openings: urine, feces, wind, or semen; and sleep when it removes the intellect.

Wiping upon the turban is not permissible, nor upon the cap. Wiping upon the leather socks and fabric socks is not permissible, except due to an enemy from whom one practices taqiyya, or snow from which one fears for the feet — then the leather socks take the place of splints and one wipes upon them.

A'isha narrated from the Prophet (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) that he said: The most severe in regret on the Day of Resurrection will be the one who sees his wudu upon the skin of someone other than himself.
And A'isha said: That I wipe upon the back of a wild donkey in the waterless desert is more beloved to me than that I wipe upon my leather sock.

key_terms.التقية: Taqiyya — dissimulation practiced by Shia Muslims under threat of harm from an enemy
key_terms.الجبائر: Al-jaba'ir — splints or bandages; the only case where wiping over a covering is valid
key_terms.الحسرة: Al-hasra — intense regret or remorse, especially on the Day of Judgment
key_terms.الخفين: Al-khuffayn — the two leather socks; wiping over them is the central legal dispute here
key_terms.الطرفين: The two openings — the private parts (front and back), source of the four wudu-nullifiers
key_terms.المسح: Al-masH — wiping as a ritual act in wudu, specifically of the feet/head
key_terms.الوضوء: Wudu — ritual ablution required before prayer

ai.seo_question: What breaks wudu according to Shia jurisprudence, and is wiping over leather socks (masah alal khuffayn) permissible?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a concise summary of Shia jurisprudential rulings on the nullifiers of wudu and the impermissibility of wiping over footwear. The Shia position, rooted in the Quran (5:6) and the Imams' teachings, holds that the feet must be wiped directly, not over shoes or socks, except in cases of necessity such as taqiyya or extreme cold. Notably, the text cites A'isha's own narration and personal statement to reinforce the Shia position against the practice of wiping over leather socks (masah 'alal khuffayn) — a practice common in Sunni jurisprudence — using her words as a rebuttal to that same tradition.

en.bilal-muhammad: The wudu is not broken but by what exits out from the two ends of urine or feces or wind or semen, and the sleep which removes the intellect.

The wiping (al-masH) is not permissible [to be done] upon the turban nor upon the cap nor upon the khuffs or the socks except for from (i.e. because of) an enemy from one is doing taqiyya or ice/snow from which one fears for the feet, so the khuffs take the place of the splints (al-jaba’ir, pl. of jabira) and one wipes upon them.

`A’isha narrated from the Prophet (s) that he said: The most severe in regret of mankind on the Day of the Resurrection will be the one who sees his wudu upon the skin of [someone/something] other than himself.
`A’isha said: That I should wipe upon the back of a wild donkey in the waterless desert is preferable to me than that I should wipe upon my khuff.
